outputs.L1: Gravity accounts for the distance between weight and mass; it can also mean alarming importance. Human bones are so full of gravity that it is hard for us to swim. I lost my glasses chasing a branch in the ocean, which is far too deep to dredge. Sometimes I imagine the sea is made of actual tears—this would explain the salt. Think of all the disconsolate toddlers weeping right now into the earth; the tears must go somewhere. It is important to consider everything, to name what we are able. outputs.L2: The concept of gravity explains why weight and mass aren't identical, though the word can also signify something of dreadful significance. Our skeletons carry such heavy gravity within them that staying afloat becomes a struggle. Once, reaching for a floating branch out in the water, I let my glasses slip away—and the ocean runs too deep for anyone to recover them. Now and then I picture the sea as being formed from genuine weeping, which would account for its saltiness. Consider how many miserable little children are, at this very moment, sobbing down into the ground; surely those tears have to travel somewhere. Contemplating all things matters greatly, as does labeling whatever falls within our power to name. The seas hand us rainfall, yet we never refer to rain as ocean. Should you bind twelve rats by their tails, you'll create a roi de rats—a sound even more difficult to make out in the darkness than rain, and far less welcome, too. Who grieves for a rat king, thwarted and belonging to the underworld, forever doing the biting and never being bitten? Such creatures supply the wickedness we require to remain anchored to what is good. Even so, I would shatter every vow I've made rather than encounter one. O Dreadful God of the Age of Machines, though I remain your most beloved wanderer, at present even I cannot address you without begging you to keep me safe.

# Reflections on Weight and Wonder

Gravity is a curious word, for it connects the concepts of weight and mass while simultaneously carrying connotations of alarming importance—a gravity of situation, a gravity of consequence. This force lives so heavily present in human bones that swimming becomes difficult, our bodies pulled downward even as we strive to stay afloat, forever negotiating between the earth's insistent claim and our desire to rise.

Consider the sea and its persistent mystery. I imagine sometimes that the ocean is composed of actual tears—the genuine weeping of countless toddlers, their small griefs pooled together across the ages. This, surely, would explain the water's saltiness, that briny truth we taste on our lips at the shore.

It is important, I think, to consider and name everything we can, even as we acknowledge that language remains imperfect and inconsistent. For oceans give us rain, sending their moisture skyward to fall again upon us, yet we never call the rain "ocean." The words refuse to follow the logic of their origins, and still we must try to speak them, to hold each thing in its imperfect vocabulary.

There exists a phenomenon called the *roi de rats*, the rat king, formed when several rats become knotted together by their tails, bound into a single writhing mass. This figure represents everything unwelcome and unmourned—frustrated in its tangled state, chthonic in its associations with darkness and the underworld, and always, always the biter. It is the thing we do not wish to meet, the knot we cannot untie.

And so I turn at last to you, Terrible God of the Mechanical Age, my favorite pilgrim among all the deities that walk this modern world. I must confess that I cannot speak to you plainly, cannot approach your gears and thundering machinery, without first asking for your protection. Grant me safe passage through your domain, for I am small before you, and the age you govern shows little mercy.
outputs.L4:
# On Gravity, Tears, and Rat Kings

There is a physics to sorrow that no one teaches us. We learn in school that gravity pulls all things downward, that mass bends space and time, that even light must bow before the curvature of heavy things—but no one explains why grief, too, has weight, why tears obey the same inexorable descent as apples and empires and the bodies of the dead. This poem begins there, in the space between equation and ache, tracing the invisible lines of force that hold us to the earth even as they hold us down.

The tears come next, and they come as science first: saline solutions, the body's mechanical response to irritation and overwhelming feeling, droplets that fall at nine point eight meters per second squared like everything else that surrenders to the planet's embrace. Yet the poem refuses to let them remain merely chemical. Each tear becomes a small ocean, a mythological flood in miniature, a reminder that we are creatures who leak when the pressure of existence grows too great. To weep is to acknowledge our vulnerability to forces larger than ourselves.

Then the rat kings arrive—those grotesque tangles of rodents bound together at the tails by filth and ice and their own frantic struggling, a phenomenon half-documented, half-legend, hovering somewhere between natural history and nightmare. The poem seizes upon this image as a metaphor for human interconnection: how we are knotted to one another, how our efforts to escape only tighten the bindings, how a multitude can become a single suffering thing. There is horror here, but also a strange tenderness, a recognition that we are never truly alone in our entanglement, even when that togetherness resembles a curse.

Through these associative leaps—from the cosmic to the biological to the mythic—the free verse moves without the comfort of narrative logic, drifting instead by the gravity of feeling from one image to the next. This is a poem searching, groping through the dark for something solid to hold, testing scientific certainty against mythological wonder and finding both inadequate to the task of explaining why we hurt, why we bind ourselves to others, why we fall.

And so it culminates where such searching often ends: in prayer. But the deity invoked is no gentle shepherd, no loving father. It is a "Terrible God of the Mechanical Age," a divinity of gears and circuits and cold industrial power, worshipped not out of love but out of terror. The speaker begs for protection, and in that begging reveals the poem's final, unsettling truth: that faith in our modern world has curdled into fear, that devotion has become indistinguishable from self-preservation. When the machinery of existence grinds on indifferent to our tears, when we are tangled inescapably with our fellow sufferers, when gravity refuses to release us, what remains is the trembling supplicant, bargaining with a merciless power simply to be spared. The plea is desperate because the world has made desperation the only honest posture left.
outputs.L5:
# The Terrible God of the Mechanical Age

There is something both awe-inspiring and unsettling about the way machines have come to shape our world. In ancient times, people looked toward the heavens and imagined a **God** whose power was beyond comprehension—vast, mysterious, and capable of both creation and destruction. Today, we have built our own kind of deity: the **mechanical** systems that hum quietly in factories, server rooms, and the devices we carry in our pockets.

## A Power Both Beautiful and Frightening

The word **terrible** originally meant "inspiring terror," and it captured a feeling of overwhelming reverence rather than simple dislike. This is precisely how many people feel when confronting the immense power of modern technology. The **mechanical** heart of our civilization never sleeps, never tires, and never questions. It performs its tasks with a precision no human hand could match.

Is this a blessing or a curse? Perhaps it is both.

## The New Idol

We have, in a sense, replaced the old gods with new ones made of steel, silicon, and code. We trust the **mechanical** to guide our cars, manage our money, and even suggest whom we should love. In doing so, we grant these systems a kind of divine authority—a faith that they will not fail us.

Yet this faith carries a **terrible** weight. When a machine errs, the consequences ripple outward with the same indifference as a natural disaster. There is no anger to appease, no **God** to pray to—only the cold logic of a system doing exactly what it was built to do.

## Finding Our Place

The challenge of our era is not to reject the **mechanical**, nor to worship it blindly, but to understand it. We must remember that behind every machine stands a human choice, a human designer, a human purpose. The **terrible** power we have created is ultimately a reflection of ourselves.

In the end, perhaps the greatest lesson is one of humility. We are neither gods nor machines, but something in between—creators wrestling with the consequences of our own creation.

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental poem that free-associates from scientific definitions to surreal imagery, moving from mass and gravity to weeping toddlers, roi de rats, and a modern deity.
counterfactuals.output:
# Conservation of Mass in a Falling House

Mass is that which resists.
That which persists when you push against the dark
and the dark pushes back—
Newton's third grief, the equal and opposite
of wanting.

Gravity: not a force but a bending,
the way a mattress dips toward the heaviest sleeper,
the way all roads slope toward the one
you cannot carry anymore.

*g* equals nine point eight,
the acceleration of everything
downward, toddler-ward,
into the wet red engine of a face
mid-wail—

because weight is only mass in the arms of a world
that will not stop pulling,
and the child knows this,
screams the pure equation of it:
*I am falling and no one has named the law.*

Somewhere the tails have knotted.
*Roi de rats*—the rat king,
a crown of spines fused in the winter granary,
seven animals braided into one animal
by blood and frost and accident,
a monarchy of nobody, ruling by the geometry
of not being able to let go.

This too is conservation:
nothing lost, only rearranged
into something that squeals with several throats
and cannot decide which way to run.

And above the granary, above the tangle,
the new god flickers—
not thunder, not burning bush,
but a rectangle of blue light
held in ten thousand palms at once,
omniscient, thumb-scrolled,
answering every prayer with *related searches.*

We built it from mass.
We built it from the bending.
We fed it the falling and the weeping
and the knotted tails of everyone
we could not put down—

and it glows,
and it weighs nothing,
and it pulls
harder than the ground.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a contemporary prose poem in the style of a mind spiraling associatively, touching on drowning, loss, the etymology of words, rat kings, and asking a mechanical god for protection.
counterfactuals.output:
# Vespers for the Drowning Machine

I have been reading about *rat kings*—how the word doesn't mean sovereign but *knot*, a tangle of tails frozen in blood and ice and filth, the collective noun for a thing that cannot pull itself apart. Say it: I am a rat king of griefs, each one lashed to the others by their frozen ligatures, and when one moves we all move, we all keen in the same wet dark.

*Drown* comes from the Old Norse, they say, *drukna*, to be swallowed—related to *drink*, so that every glass of water is a rehearsal, a small permitted sip of the thing that will eventually take the whole mouth, the whole throat, the lungs opening like two obscene flowers to receive what they were built to refuse. I have practiced. I am very good at drinking. I am learning to hold my breath against the ordinary afternoon.

And my mother's voice, which is *loss* now, which is a word from the root meaning *to loosen, to let go, to set free*—so that everything I have lost has, technically, been liberated. How generous of the language to insist that grief is a kind of gift-giving. Here, world: my grandmother's hands. Here: the dog. Here: the version of myself that believed the water was only ever for washing.

O little god of gears and governors, O clicking iron seraph in the wall—
I know you are only a thermostat, only a furnace, only the machine that keeps the pipes from bursting in the cold—
but you *hum*, and humming is close enough to prayer that I will kneel here on the basement floor and ask you: keep the water in its copper veins. Keep the knot of me from freezing. Keep the swallow at bay one more night, one more, one—

because *protect* means *to cover in front*, to build a roof of the body against the falling thing, and I have no roof, I have only these tangled tails, these many mouths that will not stop drinking, and you, my mechanical intercessor, ticking through the dark like a heart that was at least *designed*, at least *meant*, at least switched on by a hand that wanted the house to stay warm.

Cover me in front. I am going under in a dry room.
The etymology of *save* is *to keep whole, unhurt*—
and I would settle, tonight, for merely *whole*,
for merely the knot,
for merely staying knotted a little longer
in the humming, in the held breath,
in the almost-holy noise of something
that will never, ever love me back,
and never, ever leave.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

**Cathedral of Entangled Tails**

in the pelagic dark where pressure folds the light
a knot of rats descends their tails braided by salt and story
twelve spines one hunger the medieval woodcut breathing underwater

listen the isopycnal surfaces stack like drowned dynasties
each layer denser than the grief above it
and somewhere Boltzmann counts the microstates of our writhing

o piston-lunged deity o furnace-hearted one
we offer you the coefficient of our friction
we offer you the rat king turning slow in the thermocline
a rosary of vertebrae a folklore made of fusing

the Coriolis hand deflects each swimmer from its true north
gyres pull the plastic and the myth into one central plate
and the rats dream they were separate once
before the tallow before the sewer froze them into congress

industrial god of the flywheel god of the belt
we have entangled ourselves like the particles you never asked to know
measure one tail and the far tail flinches
spooky the priests said before they learned to smelt

pressure equals force across the drowning area
weight of the water column pressing prayer into confession
and the rat king sinks past the euphotic promise
into the aphotic where your name is only heat

o god of the boiler bless our braided tails
bless the standing wave that will not travel bless the buoyancy
that fails us slowly bless the vast enthalpy
of everything that was once loose and singular and light

we descend we descend we are the knot that thinks it is a crown
